articleTitle: New TLM models for thin structures
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A new TLM model for thin finite conductivity films is described. The basis of the method is the representation of the boundary by an equivalent one-dimensional lossy transmission line which is integrated into a parallel three-dimensional TLM code called PSTRIPES. Two applications of the model are considered. The first is an EMC problem where the authors compute the response to a hybrid structure. The other is a microwave problem where we model a travelling-wave tube with graphite loading.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: FEM analysis and modelling of busbar systems under AC conditions
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors present a quite general model of busbar systems taking into consideration skin and proximity effects and any possible connection of subconductors. The proposed approach is based on a finite element electromagnetic field computation to deduce the impedance matrix and on a successive network analysis to predict the device behaviour. This technique can be used for simulating busbar systems under periodic operating conditions even if the supply quantities are affected by a significant harmonic content. The method is based on the assumption of linearity of the system, which is usually verified except under some short circuit conditions in presence of ferromagnetic enclosures. An analysis of two 3-phase industrial busbar systems having respectively one and two subconductors per phase is developed. The predicted results are in good agreement with the experimental ones.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dynamic analysis of voltage excited tubular linear induction actuators
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Describes a strategy to deal with dynamic analysis of electromechanical devices energized by voltage sources. The coupling between external electric circuits, which may include power electronics, and the internal electromagnetic field involving saturation, eddy current and movement, is investigated. A combination of parabolic curve fitting technique and the secant method which has its special physical explanation here minimizes the CPU time consumed. An embryonic form of a tubular linear induction actuator (TLIA) is used as an example and its simulated results are in good agreement with experimental ones.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computation of electromagnetic switching transients in a substation
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A computer program that calculates the electromagnetic radiation produced by switching transients within a high voltage substation is described. Sections of the substation circuit are assumed to act as antennae over a perfect ground plane. This should give a worst case estimation of the field amplitudes within the confines of a substation. These results may be used for electromagnetic compatibility studies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Transition rectangular to circular waveguide by means of rectangular guides
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The step transitions between rectangular and circular waveguides using rectangular intermediate steps have shown to be a good solution for matching these two different types of guides, from both electrical performance and size point of view. The electrical behaviour can be analyzed very accurately, as has been shown, with the algorithm used in the paper, in a very reasonable time, since the optimization of the integration and the separation of the frequency dependent and frequency independent parts of the problem have been included in the software. Also multistepped transitions, with two or more steps, and resonant structures can be analyzed very accurately as has been shown.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Accurate finite element software for microwave and optical waveguides
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: For rapid and accurate analysis of microwave and optical waveguides, users need a CAD-oriented interface to the underlying method. The authors describe an accurate method based on Berk's (1956) powerful variational result for resonators and waveguides. Particular attention is given to the user interface, whose role is to protect everyday users from all contact with the lengthy mathematical and numerical solution details connected with this or similar formulae. In the current package called POMME (Program for Optical and Microwave Modal Evaluation), the first steps are to input the cross-section of a particular waveguide on the graphics workstation and to give the material properties in each subregion. General-purpose automatic mesh-generation software is used to split the subregions into small finite elements where the unknown H field components are represented by linear combinations of first order shape functions. The fields at all the nodes can finally be obtained by solving a large (but sparse) global matrix problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Wide-band optimization of E- and H-plane waveguide junctions
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors present a user-oriented design tool for E- and H-plane lossless waveguide junctions. The circuits considered are bounded by two parallel conducting planes and by one or more cylindrical sidewalls of arbitrary shape. The P-ports are placed on rectangular waveguide sections, which, in the frequency band of interest, permit the propagation of interest, permit the propagation of the dominant TE/sub 10/ mode only. They assume that the medium is homogeneous, isotropic and lossless. The algorithm has two distinguishing features: the inclusion of a very efficient code to perform the analyses needed to evaluate the error function; and the use of a perturbational technique to obtain its sensitivity to geometrical deformations. Both features, which are discussed, contribute to keep CPU times within reasonable limits, making feasible the design of complicated junctions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Acceleration of TLM through signal processing and parallel computing
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The transmission line matrix method (TLM) has been used extensively for modelling closed electromagnetic structures by authors such as by Johns (1986). Johns matrix techniques are now extending its applications to partially open structures, and the modelling of planar antenna configurations becomes feasible. The TLM process yields the time response of a structure to impulsive excitation, which must usually be transformed into the frequency domain using Fourier transform techniques. The authors propose and describe two complementary procedures designed to significantly reduce computational expenditure. The first exploits the localised nature of the TLM process through parallel processing (implementation on the connection machine), and the other is based on the numerical processing of the TLM output using the Prony-Pisarenko method. Both measures may be applied to accelerate other time domain methods such as FD-TD.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Finite element solutions to 3D waveguide problems using the magnetic vector potential
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors use a formulation based on the Lorentz gauge, which is extended to solve 'high' frequency cavity and waveguide problems. The magnetic vector potential is used throughout space, along with the electric scalar potential. However, the Lorentz gauge can be used to decouple these equations, leading to a more efficient solution algorithm. Since the equations are properly gauged, there are no 'spurious' modes arising (in particular in an eigenvalue solution to cavity problems). Unlike field variables (E or H) the magnetic vector potential is continuous between materials of differing permeability, permittivity and conductivity. It is therefore ideally suited to problems involving waveguide discontinuities and to waveguides with permeable and lossy dielectric loads.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Symbolic computation as a basis for numerical methods
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Symbolic algebra is supplanting its traditional counterpart as the foundation of numerical methods in engineering. It has allowed production of refined techniques, e.g. new finite elements and improved perturbation methods. While it permits direct solution of some new field problems, its main impact is likely to remain in the creation and refinement of numerical tools. After surveying past applications, currently common systems and languages for computer algebra are reviewed briefly.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The prediction of radiation levels from printed circuit boards by means of the finite difference time domain method
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The necessity for the control and minimisation of unintentional electromagnetic emissions from electrical systems has long been appreciated and much skilled effort is spent on EMI suppression. Due to the complexity of the problem, however, very little in the way of CAD tools is available to help the designer. A technique is described, based on the finite difference time domain technique, whereby the radiation levels from digital circuits may be predicted. The predicted results are compared to measurements for a trial configuration.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Time domain modelling: integral equations, finite differences and experimental results
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Describes the fundamental assumptions present in two numerical time domain methods based on the electric (or magnetic) field integral equations and Maxwell's equations. The cause of late time instabilities in the former is analysed, and a practical and effective method of eliminating them is presented. Numerical results of the methods for some idealised problems are presented. Discrepancies in the decay envelope of the backscattered pulses are attributed primarily to the finite thickness of the FDTD (finite difference time domain) plates, as opposed to the infinitely thin structures used in the integral equation representation. Upon modifying the conductivity in the FDTD plate model to make the plate thin, in the sense that its thickness is comparable to its skin depth, significantly improved agreement is obtained. Future work will address the cause of this implied resistivity in the integral equation model.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Numerical simulation of field-to-wire coupling problems using transmission-line modelling
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Modifications to the transmission-line modelling method are described which greatly improve the field-to-wire coupling capabilities. Results are presented to demonstrate the use of the method to simulate lossy material and coupling of fields to wires inside boxes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer-aided optimization of rare-earth permanent magnet actuators
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The application of high energy permanent magnets such as NdFeB and PrFeB, offers the potential for increasing the power/weight capability of many forms of limited motion actuator. The authors describe a CAD package which offers two approaches to optimization, the first of which involves the scanning of the 'design space' by incrementing one or more of the leading design parameters within a pre-specified range, whilst the second employs a penalty function constrained optimization method to minimize an application specific objective function. Both use nonlinear reluctance networks to model the actuator whose design is to be synthesized. Two case studies are presented to demonstrate the utility of the package, the first of which is concerned with the design of a limited angle torque motor for maximum torque/amp and torque/inertia whilst the second is a short-stroke linear voice-coil actuator optimized for minimum copper loss, both being validated experimentally.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analytical determination of the instantaneous airgap field in a brushless permanent magnet DC motor
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: An analytical technique is presented for predicting the airgap field distribution in radial-field topologies of brushless motors under any load condition, accounting implicitly for the corresponding stator winding current waveforms and the effects of stator slot-openings. It is based on a 2-D analysis of the airgap/permanent magnet region, and combines an analytical calculation of the armature reaction field with an analytical prediction of the phase current waveforms and the field produced by the magnets to permit the instantaneous field distribution to be predicted under any steady-state load and specified commutation strategy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: CLASP-a new, general-purpose method of moments scattering code
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: CLASP (Culham Laboratory Advanced Scattering Program) is a new computer code for the simulation of the electromagnetic scattering from metallic, dielectric and magnetically permeable bodies of arbitrary shape. The code is based on Kirchhoff's integrals in the frequency domain for the scalar and the vector electromagnetic potentials, and the method of boundary finite elements (also known as the method of moments), in a Galerkin formulation. By these means, the analytical expressions for the electromagnetic field are converted into a system of linear algebraic equations, which are solved to find the current density at the given frequency on all parts of the scattering body. The scattered electromagnetic field may be calculated directly once these currents are known.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A finite element technique for voltage driven devices
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors present a 2D finite element technique for predicting the steady-state alternating behaviour of electrical devices where the terminal voltages and the supply circuits are assigned (voltage driven devices). The method, which also takes into account the eddy current effects, expresses the induced electromotive forces in terms of the unknown magnetic vector potential and so inserts the circuit equations into the field problem. The proposed technique allows for the connection of complicated external networks of voltage sources and dissipative parameters. The introduction of fictitious electromotive forces related to a single conductor makes circuit manipulation easier. The possibilities of imposing supply currents and of neglecting eddy currents are included. The proposed procedure is applied to the behaviour of multiconductor busbar systems. A three-phase system under short circuit conditions; and an AC electromagnet with shaded rings under rated and reduced supply conditions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new finite element scheme for optical temporal soliton analysis
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: In order to get insights for more complex nonlinear scalar or vectorial simulations, which could include simultaneous spatial and temporal soliton analysis, a comparison among the most common two step-by-step finite element method (SbS/FEM) algorithms, the FE scheme and the well known split step/Fourier method (SS/FM), has been performed. To reach this goal, as a model, the dimensionless nonlinear Schrodinger equation, associated to the Kerr nonlinearity type, has been adopted. This equation describes optical temporal solitons propagating through a nonlinear monomode optical fibre (NMOF). From a numerical point of view this example constitutes a very good test provided that the collision can create numerical instabilities due to the complex shape adopted by the pulses during the colliding interaction.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Time domain integral equation methods for nonlinear systems
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Reviews the application of time domain integral equation (TDIE) methods to the prediction of current flow and radiated fields in antenna and scatterer systems with nonlinear loads. Typical applications include the prediction of currents and voltages induced in printed circuit boards by external fields and the prediction of radar cross section (RCS) of wire antennas with nonlinear loads.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power transformer design with finite elements-a company experience
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The implementation of computer aided drawing and design techniques for many aspects of mechanical and electrical design and manufacture is widely accepted in many companies. However, in the power industry the use of modern electromagnetic design software, such as finite element programs, has not been widespread. There are two main reasons for this difference in emphasis. One is the fact that commercially available electromagnetic software has only recently begun to appear as a mature product and the other is that this type of software requires a high degree of commitment in application and understanding to ensure its success. The paper gives an account of the successful application of this type of software in industry and discusses, using example test cases, the merits of its use and the types of problems that are presented when using it in the power transformer design arena.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of finite element methods to the modelling of field ingress to structures
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The problem of the ingress of electromagnetic waves to structures is of central importance in the field of electromagnetic compatibility (EMC). British Aerospace (Dynamics) Limited have responsibility for EMC in all company products. Computational electromagnetic (CEM) techniques can be applied to both assessment of problems arising in existing systems, and to good initial EMC design of products. The CEM techniques that can be applied to the problem may be broadly classified on the basis of the method by which they are derived from Maxwell's equations. Methods based on integral equations often using the method of moments are ideal for solving radiated field problems, particularly for conductors. They can be used to compute the incident field strength at the target equipment, and currents flowing on the outer surface. For problems of field ingress to structures, especially if the interior geometry is complex, differential methods are more suitable. Techniques such as finite difference and finite element methods can be employed. Both have different advantages and drawbacks. The application of the finite element (FE) method for modelling field ingress to a simple structure at VHF and UHF frequencies is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Identification of L-M-models of electrical machines by means of the FE-method with application to converter-fed synchronous machine problems
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A very efficient and flexible method for the identification of L-M parameters of electrical machines based on the finite element method is presented. The spatial dependency of the mutual inductances is determined and the Fourier analysis is then used to separate their spatial harmonics components. They are used for steady-state and transient analysis of currents in the windings and the damper bars of a synchronous machine under normal and fault operating conditions. The graphic interface being used for the input of windings structure makes the program easy to use even by the less experienced personnel. The fundamentals of the method and the numerical results are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: TLM techniques in microwave ovens analysis: numerical and experimental results
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Since, from an electric point of view, food can be modelled as an inhomogeneous complex dielectric body of irregular shape, an accurate analytical method is required to predict the electromagnetic field distribution inside it. To that purpose, the TLM method proves to be the most efficient; in the present contribution the method has been used to evaluate resonant frequencies of a commercial microwave oven, empty and filled with a phantom simulating the dielectric characteristics of a biological tissue; moreover the electric field distribution inside the phantom has been obtained. Theoretical results have been compared with experimental measurements performed by a vector network analyzer and infrared thermography obtaining a good agreement.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Mode matching analysis of combined circular and coaxial structures loaded with dielectrics
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The formulation described by Tun et al. (1987) for circular guides is extended to include interaction with coaxial waveguides placed in line with the circular guides. Both types of waveguides may either be partially or fully loaded with dielectrics. For loaded waveguides the intrinsic eigenmodes of the cross-sections are evaluated prior to mode matching. The analysis has been confined to structures excited by modes with unity azimuthal index such as the dominant TE/sub 11/ mode of the circular guide. However, the formulation is valid for all indices. As the technique is implemented in a general way, the same software can be used to analyse components such as corrugated horns with ring-loaded slots or arbitrarily shaped slots (V shaped), coaxial couplers, multiband feeds, closely spaced feed-subreflector assemblies, etc.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Nonlinear modeling of microwave heating problems
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A new nonlinear numerical modeling is proposed to analyze microwave heating problems. It is based on an iteration between solving the Maxwell's curl equations and computing the heat conduction equation. The temperature dependences of the permittivity, permeability and conductivity are considered in the calculation, so that more accurate results can be obtained. The two-dimensional finite difference time domain (FD-TD) formulas are used to solve the nonlinear equations. To verify the method numerical examples are provided.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A comparative study of a class of FFT-based methods for the computation of electromagnetic scattering from 2 and 3D objects
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A systematic comparison of three methods based on the different ways of generating variational basis functions in van den Berg's algorithm is conducted. The MSIT is a matrix interpretation of the spectral iteration technique; the CGFFT (conjugate gradient fast Fourier transform) is obtained by an appropriate choice of basis function. A third choice, based on a generalized Neumann series (GNS) expansion of the inverse of the integral equation operator is proposed. Test cases in both 2 and 3D for a wide range of dielectric problems show that the GNS is more efficient that either the MSIT or the CGFFT irrespective of material composition, size or shape.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Visualization of electromagnetic phenomena
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Numerical methods based on time-domain integral or differential formulation of electromagnetic problems are adequate to produce computer animated movies. The use of several of these tools to produce animated displays of electromagnetic field propagation and interaction is considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Portable interactive-graphics software for generation of the inputs to moment-method and GTD programs
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Two interactive-graphics input programs for high-frequency electromagnetic modelling packages are described. One (WGM) generates segmented wire-grid input for the method of moments; the other (GENIE) generates a set of flat plates for the geometrical theory of diffraction. These were written in FORTRAN-77, using the standard GKS (graphical kernel system) graphics commands in order to maximise the portability and maintainability of the software. The programs contain several features to ease the input of the physical structure of the object to be modelled and its subsequent subdivision into wire segments or GTD plates of appropriate dimensions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new variational finite element analysis of microwave and optical waveguides without spurious solutions
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The method presented can deal with waveguides of arbitrary cross-section and transverse inhomogeneity, including anisotropy and loss (or gain). It gives directly solutions for the (complex) propagation constant and totally eliminates the spurious solutions which ordinarily appear interspersed with the correct results of many vectorial finite element formulations. Additionally, efficiency has been maximized by using only two vector components to describe the problem. A very efficient new solver for the sparse nonsymmetric matrix eigenequation has been developed for the formulation and it is also reported. This new finite element method with the efficient matrix solver which drastically reduces computing time and storage has been thoroughly tested showing its effectiveness and applicability.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improvement on the convergence of modified discrete convolution method for scattering from a finite periodic structure
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A modified discrete convolution method (MDCM) is presented. It is based on formulating the conventional discrete convolution method (DCM) and zeroing the Frobenius norm of the iterative matrix. The storage space and the multiplicative operations of MDCM are almost the same as that of DCM, but the former is convergent more stably than the latter. This modified method is suitable to the electromagnetic scattering or radiation problems with electrically large geometry, especially to the problem with a finite periodic structure.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An axisymmetrical finite element-boundary element coupling method for the study of circuit breakers
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Rotating arc circuit breaker modeling requires the computation of the magnetic induction on the arc in order to estimate the Laplace force. An accurate modeling has to take into account the eddy currents and the magnetic saturation in axisymmetrical geometry. A finite element-boundary element coupling method is considered to deal with open boundary problems. Finite element domains can be used for conducting and nonlinear magnetic materials while boundary element domains are used elsewhere, that is mainly for the air. Numerical stability of the finite element method is insured by the use of an auxiliary potential equal to the vector potential divided by the radius. Boundary integrals required by the BEM involve elliptic functions which prevent any analytical treatment. Numerical integrations are made by an adaptative scheme which provides good accuracy of results. As the nonlinear character of the system prevents the use of complex formalism, even for sinusoidal excitations, transient analysis is made by using an Euler implicit scheme for time integration. The computed induction provides the time evolution of the force acting on the arc.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Decoupling for magnetostatics
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Outlines a semi-analytic technique for simplifying the assembly and solution of systems of equations resulting from the use of the boundary integral method in magnetostatics. The analysis can be extended to cover the nonlinear domain but attention is restricted to linear magnetostatics. The method is based on domain decomposition and the superposition of potentials. This significantly reduces computational complexity and allows 'large' problems to be solved more easily on multiprocessor systems. The author details a method which is essentially 'cubic', i.e. doubling the number of processors yields an eightfold 'speed-up'. This is achieved by apportioning the solution space to subdomains upon which decoupled solutions can be obtained. The fully coupled solution can then be determined by linear relations based on the superposition of decoupled potentials. Algorithms based on this method are being implemented on an Intel Hypercube at Daresbury Laboratory.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling of absorptive boundaries in the TLM model
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: An important engineering problem is the prediction of the microwave scattering properties that depend on the physical shape of an object or device. A method that has been developed relatively recently is based on the transmission line matrix (TLM) model. In this method, space is divided into discrete cubic cells by a deformed rectangular mesh. Propagation of a wave from one side of a cell to the other is modelled as propagation of a wave along a link transmission line connecting the cube faces. In three-dimensions, there are three transmission lines per cell, forming a matrix with junctions or nodes in the centre of each cell. The numerical method used to solve the matrix reduces to copying pulse amplitudes from one node to adjacent nodes then multiplication by the scattering matrix at each node. This method produces as output a time series of field strength at each node.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The generalized multiple technique in spectral domain
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A combination of the generalized multipole technique and spectral domain technique is proposed. It is applicable to electromagnetic scattering in the presence of stratified media interfaces. Only the equivalent multipole sources corresponding to the scatterer are necessary since a Green's function in the spectral domain includes the interface effect. Numerical examples are given for underground 2D scatterers consisting of conducting material or dielectric material.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new general method for numerical solution of linear integral equations in numerical electromagnetics
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The method minimizes mean square error of the approximate solution. It is different from classical least square method which minimizes the residual of integral equations. The method is presented for the general, one-dimensional case, and in the case of surface integral equations, which are of particular interest in electromagnetics. Typical results presented for charge distribution over a prolate ellipsoid and current distribution along a wire scatterer show that, by proper choice of the integral equation and basis functions, the method converges very fast to the exact solution.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimal design of radiating structures
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors examine a shape identification problem governed by the Helmholtz equation for antenna design optimisation. Results are given for the minimisation of the reflection coefficient of axisymmetrical antennas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Detailed self-consistent modelling of the lateral optical fields in an N-substrate InP/InGaAsP constricted-mesa laser diode for microwave modulation applications
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: High optical confinement means that many modes may be guided in the lateral direction, and it is possible for many of these modes to lase. A second problem is caused by the homojunction regions formed either side of the active layer. Current spreading at high injection can cause these regions to become forward biased. This leakage current does not contribute towards light production, and causes sub-linearity of the light-current characteristic, giving rise to harmonic distortion. A self-consistent model of the static electrical and optical properties of the constricted mesa laser has been developed to examine these problems The model includes the effects of current spreading in the p-type mesa layer and allows for the possibility the several lateral optical modes may lase simultaneously.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Size reduction of the H-field finite element formulation for waveguide structure analysis
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: An improved finite-element technique has been presented, capable of solving waveguide problems with very coarse meshes. The new technique uses the magnetic field vector H, and improves the accuracy of the obtained solutions, by optimizing an exponential parameter instead of refining the finite-element mesh. The validity and efficiency of this technique has been shown in the analysis of hollow and dielectric-loaded metallic waveguides, where the number of mesh-unknowns is reduced by 50-70%. Also, the computing time is reduced to roughly one-tenth of that required for the conventional H-field formulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer aided design of precision slotted waveguide array antennas
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A computer aided design package for the synthesis of rectangular waveguide broadwall slot array antennas has been described. The package differs from preceding contributions in this area in that the self admittances of the slots are computed, rather than taken from a data bank of measured values. The self admittance computations rely on the use of the moment method, which is known to be potentially as accurate as the best measurements is evaluating slot self scattering effects. The resultant CAD package has been applied to the design of a linear slotted-waveguide array. Near field measurements on the array have been shown to be is reasonable agreement with theory, once certain constructional limitations are taken into consideration.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Novel analytical technique to solved 2D-boundary value problems of non-orthogonal domain boundaries
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Many boundary value problems in electromagnetics involve non-orthogonal contours, and are therefore difficult to solve analytically. A simple mathematical formulation is proposed making is possible for some potential problems of this kind to be solved by non-orthogonal expansion.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electromagnetic modelling of impedance-loaded dielectric space-frame radomes
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: For the EM design phase involving parametric studies on the effect of radome geometry, strut cross-section and compensation designs, a fast method of evaluation is required. The authors describe a radome scattered field solution based on an oblique MOM solution which gives all scattered field components at any combination of the four incidence and scattering angles, including the depolarised fields, for arbitrary cross-section shape inhomogeneous cylinders of infinite length. These fields are used to find the full 3D scattered field solution for finite length cylinders, with very general incident field conditions, via plane wave spectrum ideas. This provides an accurate solution to the problem of finding the radome scattered field at any angle in space when the enclosed antenna is not restricted to being a large reflector. Complete antenna patterns may be generated as the radom rotates relative to the antenna, thereby allowing the modified sidelobe envelope to be seen for all antenna pointing directions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparison of RCS prediction techniques, computations and measurements
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The National Aerospace Laboratory NLR and the TNO Physics and Electronics Laboratory have started a research project to acquire capabilities to predict the radar signature of aircraft, since the requirement of low radar cross section (RCS) has become a critical driver in the design of military aircraft. The research concerns the development of RCS prediction techniques as well as the assessment of the capabilities of these techniques. The authors evaluate the capabilities of three prediction techniques by calculating the monostatic RCS of the geometry given. This geometry can be considered as a generic model of a wing with an engine inlet of a fighter aircraft. The evaluation includes a discussion of practical and numerical aspects. The following prediction techniques are applied: a 3D high frequency method, a 3D boundary element method and a 2D finite difference time domain method.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computation of elliptic integrals of the third kind in high-frequency EM scattering problems
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The expression for the surface-ray fields in the UTD formulation is such that in the computation the antenna characteristics over these scatterers, these elliptic integrals are accessed repeatedly, typically up to 1 million times. Hence, it is desirable to determine the computational efficiency of the various formulae vis-a-vis the nature of the scattering structures. The authors present a comparison of the accuracy, range and computational complexity of the various formulations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Calculating the radar cross section from multiple-bounce interactions
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A robust and computationally efficient method of calculating the far-field RCS in the high frequency region due to multiple-bounce interactions among any number of arbitrarily located flat polygonal plates was developed and implemented. The accuracy of the method was verified by successfully comparing the RCS calculations with measured data for a rectangular cavity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling of nonlinear active devices in TLM
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The modelling of active and nonlinear subregions of microwave structures using the transmission line matrix (TLM) method is discussed. It is shown that a correct modelling of subregions with negative real part of the conductivity is possible by lumped circuit elements connected to the TLM mesh nodes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparative study of the time-domain methods for the computer aided analysis of microwave circuits
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Three time-domain methods are widely used: the finite difference time domain method (FD-TD), the transmission line matrix method (TLM) and the spatial network method (SN). The authors have conducted a global comparative analysis of the FD-TD, TLM and SN methods. The results of the investigation are summarized. The three methods prove formally equivalent in application to the analysis of linear microwave circuits of arbitrary complexity. The objective of the study is to extend the theorem of formal equivalence of FD-TD and TLM to nonlinear applications. In principle, the time-domain algorithms enable unified full-wave simulation of microwave circuits incorporating lumped nonlinear elements. They propose a nonlinear modification of FD-TD, and investigate its relationship to two nonlinear modifications of TLM due to Johns and O'Brien (1980) and Voelker and Lomax (1980). They also determine general criteria for stable and accurate incorporation of an arbitrary nonlinear element into a linear FD-TD (or TLM) model.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimisation of the Numerical Electromagnetics Code on a four-processor Cray X-MP computer
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A standard moment-method electromagnetic field computation program (the Numerical Electromagnetics Code) was subjected to a series of modifications to improve its execution speed on a vector processing computer with four pipelines. For test problems involving computation of the near field of an array of log-periodic antennas speed improvements of up to eight times were achieved by a combination of the following techniques: code reordering to maximise vectorisability; microtasking of interaction matrix solution; and macrotasking of matrix filling and near-field computation. Micro and macrotasking are alternative techniques for scheduling of the parallel processors: the techniques required were substantially architecture-dependent, thus limiting portability of the revised code. The maximum speed achieved was one-seventh of the theoretical maximum for the computer.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Successive matching as the technique for scalarisation of waveguide vector problems
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Considers the simple example of the junction of two rectangular waveguides of different cross-sections. In accordance with the mode matching technique the authors use the two-step procedure of mode matching in the junction plane. The first step consists of matching of the field of the first waveguide with the unknown intermediate field assigned in the region possessing the width of the first waveguide and the height of the second one. The second step is the matching of that intermediate field with the field of the output waveguide. The boundary conditions on the metal junction plane are satisfied at every step.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Effect of electromagnetic interference on coupled microstrip interconnects on lossy integrated circuit substrates
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The author studies the time and frequency domain responses of a coupled microstrip line illuminated by a plane electromagnetic wave of arbitrary angle of incidence and polarization. Although the coupled microstrip on a lossy substrate provides an ideal preliminary model for the detailed investigation of externally induced electromagnetic noise in integrated circuits, currently there is no detailed study of this problem in the literature. A model which allows computation of the transmission line currents and voltages induced by the external field of arbitrary incidence at any point along the coupled microstrip line, terminated in passive load impedances, is developed. The effects of high substrate permittivity and loss tangent on the response of the microstrip to the incident field is investigated. The effect of wave polarization on wave coupling is studied against the angular orientation of the microstrip with respect to the direction of the incident wave.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer models of electrical discharges
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A numerical solution of electrical discharges in a point-plane geometry is presented. It is based on the hypotheses of laplacian electrical fields and stochastic growth. The adopted algorithm is robust and is able to reproduce several types of electrical discharge phenomena; moreover, the discharge patterns obtained fit well with experimental realizations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Radio frequency and quasi-DC mathematical modelling for the assessment of an aircraft HF antenna system
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A study of a particular airborne antenna system is described in which the prediction of the terminal reactance, as presented to the antenna tuning unit, is attempted across the HF band. Two models are considered necessary for this purpose, neither of which incorporates empirically derived information. Both models are described and each uses the method of moments. The results produced by the radio frequency (RF) model employed for the antennas and airframe are supplemented by those of a quasi-DC model which is used to calculate the stray reactances associated with the configuration of the terminals inside the aircraft. The RF model has a very high sampling density and uses NEC as the solution code. Some possible sources of error associated with each model are considered, and the results of the calculations compared with experiment. It is concluded that the accuracy attained is sufficiently good for engineering purposes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Surface integral formulation for calculating conductor loss in hollow waveguide
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The power-loss method along with a surface integral formulation has been used to compute the attenuation constant in hollow waveguides of arbitrary cross-section. An E-field integral equation has been developed for the surface electric currents which has been transformed into a matrix equation, using the method of moments. An iterative technique, i.e. Muller's method, has been used to obtain the relation between the propagation constant and frequency. The attenuation constants have been calculated and formulated for various waveguides and are in good agreement with published data.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Inverse problem on the vertical conductivity profile of a plane-layered medium
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Mambo et al. (1983, 1985) have made a simulation estimating the electron density profile of the lower ionosphere from knowledge of the VLF reflection coefficients. The fundamental equation used in the estimation is a Fredholm integral equation of the first kind with respect to the variation of the electron density and the variation of the receiving antenna output voltage, derived from Maxwell's equations. An unknown electron density profile is obtained by an iterative full wave calculation technique solving the integral equation. The method is extended to the VHF case in which the transmitted field strength varies. The vertical conductivity profile of a plane-layered medium is estimated by applying the knowledge of both reflected and transmitted field strengths. Only the case of homogeneous isotropic conductivity and TM-mode plane wave propagation is treated. However, this technique is also applicable for all propagation modes in a general anisotropic complex medium.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Anisotropic materials in electromagnetic finite element analysis
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Electromagnetic permeability, conductivity, and/or permittivity are anisotropic in many materials. The authors discuss how fully anisotropic tensors for these material properties may be used in 3D finite element analysis based on magnetic vector potential and the time integrated electric scalar potential. The tensors may have off-diagonal terms, not just diagonal terms. Besides real anisotropic tensors, complex anisotropic tensors for AC excitations are also discussed. In addition, a new method is presented for modeling nonlinear anisotropic permeability. An inductor serves as a test problem for static, complex, and nonlinear anisotropic cases; its fields calculated by finite element analysis are shown to agree with classical theory in all cases.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Variational estimation of radar cross section
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Examples are given illustrating how variational techniques may be applied to the problem of calculating the RCS of distorted (and therefore realistic) composite scatterers and of resonant-sized objects. The computing power required to predict the RCS using these variational techniques is often less than that required using more conventional techniques, especially when the RCS distribution over a small angular range is required. There is no increase in computing power required for the treatment of distorted rather than ideal scattering objects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Finite element analysis of high power striplines for beamformers
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The application of the FEM to calculate the characteristic impedance and the cut-off frequency values for the lowest order TE mode in stripline transmission lines has been described. The results obtained have been used to identify possible problems in the design of the stripline beamformers discussed by Davies (1988). The change in impedance which occurs because of the irregularly positioned dielectric supports has been evaluated. The use of a notch in the strip conductor positioned at the dielectric support is shown to reduce this impedance mismatch. The cut-off frequency of the lowest order TE modes has also been examined in both single and coupled striplines. The decrease in the cut-off frequency for identical coupled lines must be taken into account in the design of the output arms of the power splitter. Further work is currently being done to extend the analysis of higher modes to non-identical coupled lines which occur when the power splitter is no longer equi-amplitude.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparison of spectral index, semi-vectorial finite difference and vector finite element methods for the modal analysis of semiconductor optical rib waveguides
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Semiconductor rib waveguides, a typical example of which is illustrated, now have various important applications in the field of integrated optics as passive and active devices such as bends, tapers, splitters, routing switches, laser cavities, and modulators. Since the early 1980s, the UK has seen considerable progress in the modal analysis of such waveguiding structures (including directional couplers) by the use of the vector H-field finite element (VFE) method, the semi-vectorial E-field and H-field finite difference (SVFD) methods, and the spectral index (SI) methods. The SI methods, which have been implemented on mainframes and 80286-based PCs (with and without coprocessors), have far more economical computer memory and CPU time requirements than the VFE and SVFD methods which are mainly suitable for use on mainframes, powerful workstations and 80486-based PCs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Accuracy and complexity in electromagnetic codes as applied to a GTD/UTD program
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The computer program under discussion is ALDAS which computes the radiation pattern of a low gain antenna when a conducting structure is nearby. The geometry of the structure is modelled by the use of simple shapes, flat plates and cylinders of circular cross-section with the addition of more complex shapes such as general ellipsoids for the fuselage or the main structural element. Reflections from each element of the structure are found using geometrical optics techniques. The diffracted rays are of two types, an edge diffraction where a ray striking an edge is diffracted into a cone of rays, and curved surfaces where a ray travels along a geodesic of the surface shedding rays tangentially. The procedure is a mixture of geometry (the rays must be traced) and electromagnetic theory (when the correct ray is found, GTD/UTD must be employed to find the field along the ray).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Accuracy problems and their optimal solution in FE-methods
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The error problem of the finite element method (used in electromagnetic field analysis) is discussed and an optimal solution technique proposed which invokes a new finite element formulation using surface current sheets or charges at interelement interfaces. The method in combination with a standard problem-oriented adaptive process can considerably reduce the accuracy problem with a small computational effort.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Ordinary differential equation models for eddy-currents using Fourier techniques
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Modern finite-element software enables engineers to model a wide range of eddy-current problems in both two and three dimensions. For a less general range of problems, it can be efficient and instructive to use hybrid analytical/numerical techniques, the most popular of which use Fourier analysis in either rectangular or cylindrical coordinates. An analytical circuit model of infinite current sheet systems is presented in which boundaries are approximated by Fourier symmetries. By using properties of such a system the model is extended to a bounded conducting region, where the secondary is represented by a set of harmonic windings whose currents are outside the boundary. The model is applied to the TEAM Workshop problem Felix1b, which is documented by Davey (1988), and whose own efficient numerical formulation successfully uses a Green's function approach and Fourier eigenmodal shapes. In the models presented, however, all results are analytical and were derived symbolically using Mathematica.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Boundary element analysis of electromagnetic field in cylindrical structures
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The boundary element analysis of the integral equation is a general numerical analysis method of an electromagnetic field. It has the advantage of easy treatment of an open region. The authors propose a novel combined integral equation which can be applied to general electromagnetic fields in a cylindrical structure and analyze it by the boundary element method (BEM). The integral equation does not have the difficulty of the non-physical solutions. It has some merits in that it does not contain the derivatives of the unknown quantities and the coefficient matrix of the matrix equation obtained by applying the BEM is a square matrix.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A novel method for surface-ray tracing on the nondevelopable surfaces
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors outline a method for ray-tracing over the nondevelopable convex surfaces in general, thereby removing the bottleneck in the application of the UTD. They illustrate the method by deriving the ray parameters for the case of a general hyperboloid of revolution (GHOR). The versatility of this method is emphasised by proving its applicability to ray-tracing on the ogive, hitherto unsolved due to its mathematical complexity. This method, called the geodesic constant method, can also be extended to the hybrid structures which are of considerable practical interest.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On the global interpolation of shaped reflector surfaces
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Geometrical optics (GO) synthesis of reflector antennas involve the numerical solution of a system of partial differential equations obtained by enforcing the primary field along ray tubes emanating from the feed phase-center to map after reflections onto the prescribed far field. As a result, reflector profiles defined by a discrete set of points are obtained. It is then necessary to fit an analytically defined surface to this set of data-points in order to permit the evaluation of the antenna secondary field and its check against designer specifications. The implementation of two global interpolating functions is explored.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A technique to measure the high frequency electrical impedance across mechanical joints in structures made from conducting materials
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Modern aircraft designs are becoming more and more reliant upon the use of advanced composite materials. At present, it is the carbon fibre composites (CFC) that have made the major impact. The use of CFC has resulted in a significant modification to the strategy adopted to protect the avionics contained within the airframe against the various electromagnetic (EM) threats encountered by the aircraft. The general strategy is based upon a three tier topology; (1) EM screening afforded by the airframe, (2) EM screening fitted to internal cable looms, and (3) protection contained within the equipment cases. The combination of 1-3 gives rise to a protection strategy and the effectiveness of stage 1 is determined by the electrical properties of the airframe. It is of great importance to the aircraft manufacturer to be able to quantify this in order to be able to continue to implement the optimum protection strategy. Therefore, a program of work was begun to develop a technique that could be successfully used to measure the bulk electrical conductivity of mechanical joints in conductive structures.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An efficient diakoptics based algorithm for electromagnetic field mapping
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Discusses the use of diakoptics methods for solving equivalent electrical circuits analogs of Maxwell's equations. In this work a mathematical formulation is given which allows large multielement equivalent networks to be decomposed into smaller more manageable subnetworks, comprised of elemental networks which maintain the properties of the original governing equations. Subnetworks are manipulated on a piecewise basis and then reassembled to extract the field quantities that are required. Throughout the work parallel computation techniques based on the transputer as an EM field coprocessor for a PC are exploited. Some sample results are shown for a rectangular cavity hybrid coupler.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Estimation of surface curvatures from discrete data for applications to geometrical optics
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Considers the problem of estimating the curvatures of a surface when the only given data consist of the position coordinates of a discrete set of points on the surface. This is commonly the nature of the data provided on the hulls of ships and other large structures. The formula for the radar cross section (RCS) for backscatter from a closed convex surface is given. This formula was obtained from geometrical optics.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computation of 3D eddy currents in moving conductors of electromagnetic retarders
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Deals with the 3D computation of eddy currents induced in moving conductors surrounded by a magnetic field. This requires one to establish 3D formulations devoted to the computation of eddy currents in the moving regions, and then to find a numerical method which gets rid of the oscillation appearing when solving the convection-diffusion equation with a standard Galerkin discretization. The basic hypotheses concerning the range of devices modelled are the invariance of the geometry and the physical properties of the moving parts in the direction of the speed, and a static current is flowing through the field sources. In other words, the whole physical phenomena is time independent. The electromagnetic retarders fully satisfy these hypotheses and are used to validate the numerical methods proposed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Spreadsheet solution of the wave equation
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The objective is to show how a computer spreadsheet can be used to solve the wave equation with dependence on one spatial coordinate (1-D) and time. The technique is applied to TEM transmission lines. Familiarity with the basics of an electronic spreadsheet is assumed. The spreadsheet solution of a TEM transmission line relies on the discretization of both space and time to model the propagation on a line. In addition to this, the model must properly account for the line terminations (boundary conditions), junctions of different lines, lumped element line loading, etc. The model allows one to observe a 'snapshot' of the entire transmission line at a specific instant in time, or to observe time-varying voltages at several different points on a line much like with a multi-channel oscilloscope. Implementation of these features on an electronic spreadsheet requires: discretized line equations, equations or line terminations, and equations for line interfaces. Arguably, the most effective way of presenting the above within the available space is to show a spreadsheet implementation of a sample transmission line that incorporates many types of equations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulation of three-dimensional finite-difference time domain method on limited memory systems
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors discuss techniques in the modelling of electromagnetic fields using finite difference time domain (FDTD) methods applied to 80*86-based PCs or limited memory computers. Electrical modelling of structures is currently carried out mainly in the frequency domain using empirical methods or by treating structures as two-dimensional objects. Until recently the application of finite difference methods were applied to supercomputers such as the Cray XMP and Cray II. The power of modern workstations and microcomputers offer large storage area, large memory capacity and fast CPU times. Thus it is now possible for full time domain simulations to be carried out on complex structures on base model workstations and microcomputers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A finite element method for problems with moving parts
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A new method for coupling independent three dimensional meshes together is described. The coupling is performed at their interface using Lagrange multipliers. The densities and distributions of the nodes at the interface do not need to be the same. Applications of the method to a switched reluctance motor are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Secondary strips sources for EM diffraction-near field mapping and RCS
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Analysis of EM scattering from perfectly conducting objects is achieved by a simple rigorous method to obtain both near field and far field with accuracy. The geometry of the object is modeled by breaking down the contour into a series of canonical strips where singularities due to the edges are eliminated in the solution of the integral equation (E type). The near field is plotted from the average complex Poynting vector, and the far field is calculated to obtain the RCS. Then, the wavefront dislocation is used to analyse the physical phenomenon through the active and reactive energy around the object in order to apprehend the final RCS observations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parallel finite difference-time domain calculations
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors present a parallel implementation of the finite difference time domain (FDTD) method. Part of the Fortran 8x CM-2 code is given. Results are given for its application to electromagnetic scattering from an Al cube.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integral equation solution for near-field to far-field transformation
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A simple and accurate integral equation solution is presented for computing far-field antenna patterns from near-field measurements. The equivalence principle is used to replace the aperture of the antenna by equivalent electric or magnetic currents. An E-field integral equation (EFIE) is developed to relate these equivalent currents to the near-field data. The method of moments (MoM) is utilized to transform the integral equation into a matrix one and a conjugate gradient (CG) procedure is applied to solve it numerically. Accurate far-fields over large elevation and azimuthal ranges are calculated from simple measurements based on planar and spherical scanning.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modal matching techniques in horn antenna analysis
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The modal matching technique is a powerful computer based method which exploits both the increasing processing power and the increasing memory of computers. The author describes the implementation for conical horns. The technique can be used to study any microwave or millimetrewave waveguide device or horn in which the fields can be expressed as a summation of modes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Time domain analysis of inhomogeneously loaded resonators using eigenfunction expansion
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: An alternative time domain method for the analysis of dielectric loaded cavities is described. The method stems from the frequency domain approaches based on the field expansion employing entire domain basis functions. The field in the cavity is treated as a superposition of eigenfunctions of the homogeneous Laplace equation. Each field component is expanded into a series of scalar functions and at each time step one computes the expansion coefficients rather than field values at discrete nodes. An advantage of this approach is that it leads to time domain algorithms which allows for coarser time discretization.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electromagnetic scattering by the delta boundary operator method
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The principles of the rigorous DBO (delta boundary operator) formulation of EM scattering are outlined. Then a new approximate DBO theory is developed and applied to plane wave scattering by a conducting elliptic cylinder.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Airgap induction optimisation in permanent magnet synchronous machine
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Numerical field calculations and mathematical programming methods are applied to solve constrained nonlinear optimisation problems in magnetostatic systems. The authors have used four different methods that seem to be adequate to solve optimisation problems in magnetostatic devices. These methods are based on the analysis of the sensitivity of an objective versus a design parameter; and they are used to solve the problems of obtaining a specific airgap induction distribution in a tetrapolar synchronous machine. Two solutions are proposed to modify the airgap induction shape: optimisation of the permanent magnet positions and optimisation of their remnant flux densities. These approaches allow approximation of a sinusoidal shape. The authors show the importance of the choice of the different optimisation parameters to insure a reliable use of the numerical methods.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Magnetic field FEM analysis via circuit simulators
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Establishes analogies between the analysis of electrical circuits and of magnetic fields. These analogies are not established on the ground of duality principles; rather, mathematical formulations of electromagnetic fields and electrical circuits are studied, with the aim of defining adequate electrical circuits where the formulation is numerically equivalent to the FEM formulation of the electromagnetic field. Unknown quantities in the magnetic field (vector potential in the nodes) correspond, in this equivalence, to the unknown quantities in the electrical circuit (essentially potential in the nodes of the equivalent circuit). The general theory is developed, and numerical tests are shown for two cases of linear Poisson's and diffusion equations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A 3D finite element scheme for nonuniformly loaded waveguides
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A finite element scheme for modelling three dimensional cavities and waveguides is described. The formulation used is an extension of the AV scheme (A is the magnetic vector potential and V is the electric scalar potential) which is a subset of the formulations hitherto used in the MEGA program for modelling 2 and 3D low frequency eddy current problems. The scheme allows cavities of general 3D shape, which may be loaded with arbitrary dielectrics or metallic objects to be modelled. Travelling or standing waves can be supported. Special boundary conditions are used for travelling wave problems, when it is required for instance to model scattering in a dielectric loaded section connected to two or more waveguides. These boundary conditions are obtained from the analytic expressions for fields in an ideal waveguide.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer modelling of slit-coupled microwave waveguide-cavity devices
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The authors discuss the computer modelling of microwave waveguide-cavity devices such as: split-coupled H-bridges; split-coupled E-bridges; directional couplers; fin lines; and fin line resonators. The model is based on the method of moments, eigenvector functions and the Galerkin technique. The analysis focusses on coupled-slots.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Time harmonic electromagnetic field calculation for induction motors
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A method of calculating the steady state harmonic magnetic field distribution in an induction motor is established. The time harmonic components of the magnetic field duo to rotor slotting and discrete conductors are obtained in addition to the fundamental AC component. A single finite element mesh is constructed and the material properties associated with this mesh are allowed to vary with time to account for the rotation of the rotor. The effects of currents induced by rotor motion are accounted for by including an additional term in the electromagnetic field equations which are to be solved. This method is applied to an induction motor for which the harmonic components of the magnetic field are calculated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer modelling of MM-wave integrated circuit antennas using the Nystrom method
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
