abstract: The Nystrom method can be applied to the integral equations of electromagnetics. An example of an integrated-circuit antenna on a rectangular GaAs substrate is presented. The present version of the software deals with objects having the form of polyhedra, which covers a class of integrated antennas including printed loops, dipoles and so forth, dielectric rod antennas, and tapered slot antennas. A program of experimental measurements on integrated circuit antennas, both using low-frequency scale models and at millimetre wave frequencies, is presently being undertaken.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Finite element analysis for the electro-magneto-thermal phenomena in induction devices
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: A finite element analysis of the dynamic, nonlinear and coupled electro-magneto-thermal equations, that describe induction heating devices, is presented. The crucial problem of the coupling between the electromagnetic and thermal phenomena is discussed. The results of the application of an original coupling, based on a finite element solution for a system of electro-magneto-thermal equations, are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Finite and infinite elements applied to electromagnetic scattering from arbitrary objects in 2D
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Discusses the use of a mixed finite and infinite element scheme to solve the time independent form of Maxwell's equations in 2D. A new code called SEMS (Swansea Electromagnetic Solver) has been developed with preprocessing, solver and postprocessing facilities to enable a full and useful validation of the technique. The far-fields can be determined directly from the nodal values of the infinite elements but in addition a postprocessing facility has been developed so that they can be computed from surface and/or 'volume' currents within the scatterer. Initial results of far-field are compared with analytic solutions with a view to determining criteria for the discretisation of the scatterer and the relative position of the outer boundary between the finite and the infinite elements. In addition some tentative results concerning the positioning of the centre of radiation for the infinite elements are included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The effective method for solution of the problem of diffraction on unclosed cylindrical screen
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: E-polarized wave scattering by a two-dimensional unclosed cylindrical screen is considered. There has been considerable interest in utilizing such structures as reflectors of various geometries in modern communication and deep-space satellites and ground antenna systems. The authors develop a simple effective method for solution to this problem and for calculation of various properties of such structures in the resonant frequency range.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Hankel transform domain analysis of an annular-ring microstrip antenna with an air gap
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: An accurate and efficient method is presented for computing the resonant frequencies of an annular-ring microstrip antenna with an air gap. The formulation of the problem is carried out rigorously using the full wave analysis. The method of analysis is based on Galerkin's method applied in the Hankel transform domain. The calculated results for the resonant frequencies are presented as a function of the width of the air gap and some are compared with the measured results available in the literature. Excellent agreement between theory and experiment is obtained, and the validity of the present method is confirmed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Determination of FE functionals in generalized coordinates
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Electromagnetic field problems are generally solved in terms of the electric scalar potential V and magnetic vector potential A since most of the physically measurable quantities are easily derivable from V and A. In most FEM analysis the equations for static, quasi-static or time-varying fields are first described using the electric scalar and magnetic vector potentials which are then solved using FEM. In the paper a very general conclusion is developed in the generalized orthogonal coordinate system, using the generalized unit vectors u/sub 1/, u/sub 2/ and u/sub 3/, together with the Lamee's coefficients h/sub 1/, h/sub 2/ and h/sub 3/.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of electromagnetic scattering from planar coated flat strip and infinite strip grating
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Different integral equations, based upon surface/surface and combined volume-surface formulations, are developed. For the homogeneous material coating case both surface/surface and combined volume/surface formulations are used, while for the inhomogeneous material coating case, only the combined volume/surface formulation is utilized. The electric field integral equation (EFIE), magnetic field integral equation and combined field integral equation (CFIE) are developed for the surface/surface formulation and the CFIE is developed for the combined volume/surface formulation. Both periodic and nonperiodic structures are treated in the same manner using the sampling theorem. Utilizing the respective boundary conditions, operator equations containing the equivalent currents are developed. According to the periodicity of the structure, these operator equations are formulated in the spectral domain using the Fourier transforms of the integro-differential operators. The generalized biconjugate gradient-fast Fourier transform (BiCG-FFT) method with subdomain pulse and triangle basis functions is applied to solve the operator equations numerically.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Implementation of the Numerical Electromagnetics Code NEC3 on a parallel computer
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The Numerical Electromagnetic Code (NEC) is a computer code used for analysing the electromagnetic response of an arbitrary structure consisting of wires and surfaces in free space. The analysis is accomplished by the numerical solution of integral equations for induced currents. The authors give a brief description of the structure of the NEC, describe the previous computing configuration used and the objectives in implementing the parallel version of NEC on the parallel computing system which is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computation of the currents induced on an anisotropically coated infinite wedge
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The problem of plane wave scattering by an infinite wedge with uniform, imperfectly conducting faces has as yet no general analytical solution. The author obtains a numerical solution for the problem for arbitrary incidence angle and for uniform face impedances which can be anisotropic. The equivalent electric currents on the wedge faces are determined. The magnetic field integral equation is used to formulate the problem, and a combination of physical optics (PO) and the moment method (MM) is employed to obtain a solution. This technique is essentially an extension of one employed by Burnside et al. (1975).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A FD-TD based code for teaching of electromagnetic wave propagation
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Describes an interactive PC-oriented program for teaching conceptual electromagnetic phenomena related to the propagation of uniform electromagnetic waves and their normal incidence upon multiple layers. The program allows the time-domain visualisation of the electromagnetic wave propagation and its interaction with the structure. The program can be used to study how the characteristics of the layers determine the reflected and transmitted waves as well as their standing wave patterns. Starting with this information, students can do several 'computer's experiments' like calculating reflection and transmission coefficients, depth of penetration, impedances, standing wave ratio (SWR), etc. The program is based on directly solving Maxwell's curl equations using the finite difference time-domain (FD-TD) method.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Finite element model of a foil wound choke
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Foil wound chokes are often used as output filters for switch mode power supplies. The component of current is DC, however the principle loss component is at the switching frequency (20-100 kHz). These losses are notoriously difficult to estimate especially when there is a significant air gap gap in the core. The authors present a finite element solution for estimating the AC power losses in such devices. The low frequency subset of Maxwell's equations are used (that is capacitance is neglected). They assume that there are no losses in the ferrite core to reduce the size of problem to be solved.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electromagnetic software to solve 2-D static and dynamic field problems on a personal computer
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The ROSe-Hulman ElectroMagnetics software (ROSEM) was developed with support from the Center for Computer Applications in ElectroMagnetics Education (CAEME). Although the main objective was to develop a computer tool to assist in instruction and visualization of electromagnetic phenomena, ROSEM is versatile and useful as a research tool as well. ROSEM software is targeted at IBM compatible 286-class and 386-class personal computers (PCs) with coprocessors, VGA graphics, and pointers. The choice of 286-class and 386-class computers as the target machines and the fact that the software should be intuitive and graphics oriented lead to the selection of two-dimensional (2-D) electromagnetic field problems as the class of problems to be solved by ROSEM. ROSEM employs the finite difference (FD) technique augmented by a unique grid termination algorithm to solve 2-D static and dynamic interior and exterior electromagnetic boundary value problems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Evaluation of scattering in a TEM cell by the FD-TD method
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The TEM cell is a fundamental tool in electromagnetic compatibility in that it permits one to simulate the effects of a plane wave incident on equipment under test in a region large with respect to the wavelength where the field is strictly TEM. The main restriction to the high-frequency operation of the cell arises from the cutoff of the first higher order mode. The new GTEM cell permits one to overcome this restriction. EMP effects upon electronic systems can be simulated to a great level of accuracy using various types of EMP simulators. Especially in the case of a large test object a theoretical analysis is very helpful for defining the threat level at the interfaces to the smaller subsystems, which may then be tested and hardened in a laboratory. In the paper the scattering of metallic object in a GTEM cell is analyzed and the results are compared with scattering with plane wave excitation. The FD-TD proves to be effective for any shape of scattering body with both sinusoidal and pulse excitation even if it is computer time consuming. A 2D analysis that reduces the computing time is therefore reported.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: MAGNEC: a set of additions to the Numerical Electromagnetics Code (NEC) for modelling non-perfect conductors in 2 and 3 dimensions
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: The Numerical Electromagnetics Code (NEC) can be modified to treat general dielectric and magnetic media by the introduction of magnetic wires. The use of magnetic and electric currents to model such media has been described by Govind et al. (1984). By inputting wire meshes at the interface between regions of different constitutive parameters, objects such as spheres with coatings, targets with radar absorbing material (RAM) or parts of constant dielectric can be modelled without using a volume mesh of wires. It should also be possible to model surface depressions (e.g. slots) without modelling the ground plane explicitly, just as it is possible to model protrusions by imaging.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A finite element approach for lossy waveguide analysis
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: Presents an approach which is based on an automatised E/sub z/-H/sub z/ formulation which was introduced by Aubourg et al. (1983). In this formulation the frequency is a parameter and ( alpha , beta ), the attenuation and the phase constants, respectively; are calculated through a fast iterative automatic procedure. However, a difficulty exists for a first fixed frequency. If the initial ( alpha , beta ) values, are too far from the exact ones, the method can converge to a different mode. But, after a good result, the dissipative and dispersive curves can be quickly and efficiently calculated, since the initialization is made with the same alpha and beta as the ones obtained for the previous frequency. The efficiency and validity of this approach has been examined by analysing lossy dielectric-loaded metallic waveguides which possess analytical solution, as well as, lossy image waveguides.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An improvement of the DOTIG1 code (for EM signals)
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Computation in Electromagnetics
abstract: DOTIG1 is a computer code developed for the study of the interaction of arbitrary electromagnetic signals with thin-wire structures (such as antennas) in the time domain. The authors show how the program can be extended to analyze thicker wires by using the extended boundary condition theorem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
